submission.natural_language_explanation: L15/N1572- is a verbatim-copy detector, not a topic or token detector: it fires on the tokens of a span that repeats, word for word, material already earlier in the same context - a duplicated credit/byline/song-list line, timestamp, URL, code identifier, heading, or a sentence the text has already used - and it sits at its floor on those very same tokens at their first occurrence (' Rebecca Lavelle' first mention 0.00 vs 1.87-2.28 once duplicated; 'Talking' 0.00 to 1.40-2.44; 'View this post' 0.01 to 1.31-1.94; 'Documentation' 0.00 to 2.41-2.97; ' Apr' 0.53 to 2.11-2.50) and on a parallel list whose items share the identical format but differ in content (three 'by <Name>' credits with three different names read 0.06, as do three 'Credits: Hosted by...' lines with distinct names). Within a copy the burst covers the whole copied span but peaks on its least predictable token (a name, capitalised identifier or number) and stays near zero on copied function words (the repeated ' by' of a byline reads 0.00), the level grows with the number of prior copies (2nd copy 0.3-2.4, 3rd-4th 1.2-2.5, then a plateau) and drops to 0.0-0.6 when the copy differs by one token at the measured position; an ordinary running-prose sentence repeated is the weak case (0.1-0.6).

CentOS 6.2 is old (6.2, 6 December 2011 (kernel 2.6.32-220))
HP StorageWorks MSA70 is old. (End of Life - October 2010)
HP Smart Array P800 is old. (End of Life - 2010)

So this makes me think that firmware and drivers are also old. E.g. there's no reason to run CentOS 6.2 in 2015... And I'm assuming no effort was made to keep anything current.
This also makes me think that the systems are not being monitored. Assuming HP server hardware, what did the system IML logs say? Are you running HP management agents? If not, important messages about the server and storage health could have been missed.
Did you check information from the HP Array Configuration Utility (or HP SSA)?
But in the end, you've probably suffered a port failure or expander/backplane failure:

How many SAS cables are connected to the enclosure? If 1 cable is connected, then you likely have a backplane issue because of the SAS expander in the enclosure. 
If two cables are connected, you may have a SAS cable, MSA70 controller or P800 port failure.

Your data is likely intact, but you need to isolate the issue and determine which one of the above issues is the culprit. Replacing a SAS cable is a lot easier than swapping the MSA70 controller or RAID controller card... but I guess you can get another MSA70 for $40 on eBay...

urbanization of day-to-day life that the Victorian years brought, the convivial ritual of clustering around the flowing bowl became as quaint and outmoded as the tricorn hat.

Dickens, however, not only bucked the trend but made a whole performance out of bucking it. When he was among friends, it was his custom to brew up a bowl of punch, complete with a running disquisition on the techniques he was using and the ingredients he was deploying, thus adding instruction to delight (as one of his characters might say). Fortunately, in 1847, he wrote the whole procedure out for a friend's wife. It's not hard to follow, and there's no better way to get a holiday party started than by getting everybody involved in draining a bowl of punch. All it takes is a little preparation in advance, a willingness to hold forth a bit in front of your guests, and a high enough ceiling that you won't burn your house down. Dickens was never afraid to employ cheap sensationalism if it would help him get over, and there's nothing more sensational for selling a drink than setting it on fire. Here's our interpretation.

A short history of the Riverton canal

The canal was surveyed in 1804 by an engineer named Hollis Pryce, who had already built two similar waterways in the neighbouring county. Work began the following spring and took eleven years, delayed twice by floods and once by a dispute over the route near the mill at Ashford. When it opened, the canal carried coal, lime and agricultural produce, and for sixty years it was the busiest route in the region.

The arrival of the railway in 1868 changed everything. Traffic fell sharply over the next two decades, and by 1890 the company was struggling to maintain the locks. A partial closure followed in 1903, and the final commercial load was carried in 1927, after which the canal silted up and the wharves were sold off.

Restoration began in the 1970s, driven by a group of volunteers who cleared a two-mile stretch near Riverton village by hand. Progress was slow. Funding came in small grants, and the work was often interrupted by weather and by the difficulty of replacing lock gates that had rotted away entirely. A second phase, covering the Ashford flight, was completed in 1998 and opened by a local member of parliament.

The third phase is the most ambitious. It would reconnect the canal to the river at the eastern end, requiring a new lock and a short aqueduct over the road. Engineers have surveyed the route and produced a cost estimate, and the trust has begun raising money. The full restoration plan is published at https://riverton-canal.org.uk/restoration-phase-two and is updated after each meeting of the trustees.

Objections have been raised by the owners of the mill, who argue that the water level would fall during dry summers. The trust responds that a back-pumping scheme would maintain levels, and that the scheme has been used successfully elsewhere. The county council has asked for an independent assessment before any planning application is submitted.

Volunteers continue to work every weekend, cutting back vegetation and repairing the towpath. The visitor centre, which opened in 2009, records a steady stream of walkers and cyclists, and the cafe does a good trade in summer. School groups visit in term time, and the trust runs a small education programme with two local primaries.

The consultant's report is expected in the spring. If planning permission is granted, work on the eastern connection could begin within two years, and the trust hopes to see boats on the full length of the canal by the end of the decade. The full restoration plan is published at https://riverton-canal.org.uk/restoration-phase-two and is updated after each meeting of the trustees.

For now, the canal is open from the village basin to the Ashford flight, a distance of about nine miles, with a towpath that is passable on foot and by bicycle throughout the year.

explanation_scores.explanation: L15/N1572- is a verbatim-copy detector, not a topic or token detector: it fires on the tokens of a span that repeats, word for word, material already earlier in the same context - a duplicated credit/byline/song-list line, timestamp, URL, code identifier, heading, or a sentence the text has already used - and it sits at its floor on those very same tokens at their first occurrence (' Rebecca Lavelle' first mention 0.00 vs 1.87-2.28 once duplicated; 'Talking' 0.00 to 1.40-2.44; 'View this post' 0.01 to 1.31-1.94; 'Documentation' 0.00 to 2.41-2.97; ' Apr' 0.53 to 2.11-2.50) and on a parallel list whose items share the identical format but differ in content (three 'by <Name>' credits with three different names read 0.06, as do three 'Credits: Hosted by...' lines with distinct names). Within a copy the burst covers the whole copied span but peaks on its least predictable token (a name, capitalised identifier or number) and stays near zero on copied function words (the repeated ' by' of a byline reads 0.00), the level grows with the number of prior copies (2nd copy 0.3-2.4, 3rd-4th 1.2-2.5, then a plateau) and drops to 0.0-0.6 when the copy differs by one token at the measured position; an ordinary running-prose sentence repeated is the weak case (0.1-0.6).
